result:
The city employed one person to collect sounds that were no longer being made.

It was not a prestigious position. Mara’s office occupied a former supply closet beneath the licensing department, and her annual budget was smaller than the budget for flags. Nevertheless, every Thursday she took a municipal recorder into the streets and tried to arrive before something ended.

She had captured the last mechanical bell on the number nine tram. The cough of the newspaper press before its conversion to digital. A certain revolving door, admired by nobody, that sighed in three descending notes.

Each recording required a location, a date, and a description.

**Door, revolving. Glass and brass. Reluctant.**

Her supervisor had asked her to remove “reluctant.”

“Not a technical term,” he said.

“Neither is goodbye.”

“That wouldn’t belong on the form either.”

She removed it.

In October, a man came to her office carrying an empty birdcage.

“I understand you preserve things,” he said.

“Sounds.”

“Yes.”

He set the cage on her desk. There was a little wooden swing inside, perfectly still.

Mara waited.

“My wife used to sing while she washed it,” he said. “The cage, I mean. We had a canary. After it died, she kept cleaning the cage. Every Sunday.”

“Do you have a recording?”

“No.”

“Then I’m afraid—”

“I haven’t told you what she sang.”

Mara put down her pen.

The man hummed four uncertain notes. He stopped, frowned, and tried again. The second version was different.

“There was something about a window,” he said.

They spent forty minutes looking through songs on the municipal computer. None was right. At noon, he apologized for taking her time.

“Leave your number,” Mara said.

When he had gone, she found a tiny yellow feather caught beneath the cage’s removable tray.

She put it in an envelope. There was no field for it in the database.

***

That winter the city announced that the sound archive would close.

The letter praised Mara’s dedication, then explained that the recordings could be held by the central library without the continuing expense of a collection officer.

She had six weeks to finish.

For the first five, she worked harder than she ever had. She recorded the shoe repairman’s treadle machine, the loose drain cover outside the swimming pool, the freight elevator at a warehouse scheduled for demolition. She stood in sleet to capture the rattle of a shop’s metal shutter.

On her final Thursday, she took the recorder home.

Her father lived in the downstairs room. He had once repaired watches and now struggled with buttons. Each evening, Mara helped him to the kitchen table, where he inspected the newspaper under a lamp.

He no longer remembered much of what he read, but he disliked being interrupted.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“A recorder.”

“Is it broken?”

“No.”

“Then why have you brought it to me?”

She laughed, and he smiled with the satisfaction of a man who had made a joke on purpose.

She placed the recorder beside the salt.

“What should I say?”

“Anything.”

He considered this.

“Your gutters need clearing.”

“I know.”

“The back one especially.”

“I know, Dad.”

He nodded toward the machine. “Did it get that?”

“Yes.”

“Good. You never listen.”

Afterward, they ate soup. He tapped his spoon twice against the bowl whenever he finished a mouthful. He had always done this. It had irritated Mara for thirty-seven years.

She checked the little red light.

***

On her last afternoon, the man with the birdcage returned.

“I remembered,” he said.

Mara reached for a sheet of paper.

“No, not the song.” He sat down. “The bird hated water. When she cleaned the cage, she put him in a cardboard box. He made such a fuss that she sang to cover him up.”

He was smiling.

“I’d forgotten what a dreadful noise he made.”

She gave him the envelope with the feather. He held it close to his face, then asked whether she had somewhere safe to keep it. His flat was in disorder; he was preparing to move.

They agreed it would go with the recordings to the library.

After he left, Mara packed the equipment. In the bottom drawer she found a recording from her first month: eleven minutes of a station clock being wound.

She had written, in the notes, **Mostly handling noise. Possible deletion.**

She played it.

There was the scrape of the key, then a long pause. A train arrived. Someone nearby asked whether she wanted a cup of tea. She heard her own voice, younger and brisker, saying no, thank you, she was working.

Mara rewound it.

She listened again to the offer.

Then she changed the file’s status to **Retain**, put on her coat, and went downstairs to hand in her keys.
